question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
title: Authentication vs Authorization – Java Backend Interview
direct_answer: **Authentication** answers *"who are you?"* — it verifies identity by validating credentials (password, token). **Authorization** answers *"what are you allowed to do?"* — it checks permissions/roles **after** identity is confirmed. They're sequential: authentication always comes first, because you can't grant permissions to an unknown user. The clean mnemonic for interviews: failed authentication returns **401 Unauthorized**, failed authorization returns **403 Forbidden**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand identity verification vs permission checking and their strict ordering
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Swapping the two, saying authorization checks the password, or assuming they happen simultaneously
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Tie each to its HTTP status (401 vs 403) and to Spring Security's Authentication object then GrantedAuthority checks

sections.title: Two Sequential Security Questions
sections.content:
Picture entering an office. **Authentication** is showing your ID badge at the front desk to prove you're an employee — it answers **"who are you?"** by validating **credentials** (a password, a one-time code, a token). **Authorization** is what happens next: the door system checks whether your badge opens the server room — it answers **"what can you do?"** by checking your **roles/permissions**.

The two are **sequential and dependent**: authentication must succeed **first**, because you can't decide what an unknown person may access. In a Spring app, authentication produces an **`Authentication`** object holding your identity; authorization then reads the **`GrantedAuthority`** list inside it to allow or deny each request.

The interview-ready shortcut: authentication failure → **401 Unauthorized** (you're not identified); authorization failure → **403 Forbidden** (you're identified but lack permission).

sections.title: AuthN vs AuthZ at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Authentication|~Who are you?|verify credentials|password / token|fails with 401
emerald|Authorization|~What can you do?|check roles/permissions|GrantedAuthority|fails with 403
violet|Order|~Sequential|authenticate first|then authorize|identity before permission
amber|Spring|~Where it lives|Authentication object|hasRole / @PreAuthorize|stored in SecurityContext

sections.title: Authentication vs Authorization
sections.content:
| Aspect | Authentication | Authorization |
|---|---|---|
| Question | Who are you? | What can you do? |
| Checks | Credentials (password, token) | Roles / permissions |
| Order | First | After authentication |
| Failure status | 401 Unauthorized | 403 Forbidden |
| Spring concept | `Authentication` object | `GrantedAuthority`, `hasRole()` |
| Happens | At login / per request (JWT) | On every protected resource access |

sections.title: Confused: mixing identity and permission checks
Clean: authenticate first, then authorize
When Each Applies
sections.content: **Authentication** runs when a user logs in with a password, or on each request when a **JWT/token** arrives and must be validated. **Authorization** runs on **every access to a protected resource** — a logged-in user hitting `/api/admin/users` triggers a role check. In a stateless API, authentication may happen per request (validating the token) while authorization still happens on every endpoint to confirm the user holds the required role.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Authentication = who you are** (verify credentials); **authorization = what you can do** (check roles).
- They are **sequential**: authentication first, because permissions need a known identity.
- **401 Unauthorized** = authentication failed; **403 Forbidden** = authorization failed.
- Spring stores identity in an **`Authentication`** object and checks **`GrantedAuthority`** for access.
- Keep the concerns **separate** — don't put role checks inside the login step.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Authentication and authorization sound similar but they answer two completely different questions. Authentication answers who are you — it verifies your identity by checking credentials, like a username and password or a token. Authorization answers what are you allowed to do — it checks your permissions or roles to decide whether you can access a particular resource. A simple analogy is an office building: authentication is showing your ID badge at the front desk to prove you're an employee, and authorization is whether that badge actually opens the door to the server room.

The relationship between them is important: they're sequential, and authentication always comes first. You can't decide what someone is allowed to do until you know who they are. So the system authenticates you, and only then does it authorize each action. In Spring Security, that plays out as authentication producing an Authentication object that holds your identity and your roles, and then authorization reading the granted authorities inside that object to allow or deny each request.

A clean way to lock this in for an interview is through the HTTP status codes. If authentication fails — you're not logged in or your token is invalid — the server returns 401 Unauthorized. If authentication succeeded but you don't have permission for that specific resource, the server returns 403 Forbidden. So 401 is about identity and 403 is about permission. A common mistake freshers make is swapping the two, or saying authorization checks the password, or mixing role checks into the login logic. Keeping the two concerns separate — verify identity first, then check permissions declaratively — is the clean approach.

beats.label: authentication
beats.content: Authentication asks: who are you? You prove your identity with a username and password, a JWT token, or an OAuth2 flow. Spring Security runs this in the filter chain and stores the result in SecurityContextHolder. Until this step passes, the request goes nowhere.

beats.label: authorization
beats.content: Authorization asks: what are you allowed to do? It runs after authentication, checking your roles against what the endpoint requires. In Spring Security that's @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") on a method, or hasRole() rules inside HttpSecurity. You can be fully authenticated and still get a 403 if your role doesn't match.

beats.label: sharp edge
beats.content: sharp edge: saying 'auth' without specifying which one is the giveaway. Always say authentication or authorization in full. Bonus points if you name the Spring classes: AuthenticationManager handles AuthN, AccessDecisionManager handles AuthZ.

question: What HTTP status codes should you return for authentication vs authorization failures?
title: HTTP Status Codes for Auth Failures – Java Backend Interview
direct_answer: Return **401 Unauthorized** for **authentication** failures — missing, invalid, or expired credentials ("I don't know who you are"). Return **403 Forbidden** for **authorization** failures — a known, authenticated user lacking permission for that resource ("I know who you are, but you can't do this"). The naming is historically confusing: **401 actually means *unauthenticated***. A common extra is returning **404** instead of 403 to avoid revealing that a resource exists.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you map 401 to authentication and 403 to authorization correctly despite the misleading names
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning 403 for a missing token, or 401 for a permission denial; using 200 with an error body
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note that 401 should include a WWW-Authenticate header, and that some APIs return 404 over 403 to avoid leaking resource existence

sections.title: 401 vs 403: Identity vs Permission
sections.content:
Two status codes cover auth failures, and the trick is that their **names don't match their meaning**.

**401 Unauthorized** is really about **authentication** — it means **"unauthenticated"**: the request has **no valid credentials** (missing/expired token, wrong password). The server doesn't know who you are, so it can't proceed. A proper 401 should include a **`WWW-Authenticate`** header indicating how to authenticate.

**403 Forbidden** is about **authorization** — you **are** authenticated, your identity is known, but you **lack permission** for this resource (a `USER` hitting an `ADMIN`-only endpoint). Re-authenticating won't help; you simply don't have the role.

A practical nuance: some APIs deliberately return **404 Not Found** instead of 403 to avoid revealing that a protected resource even exists (preventing enumeration). And never return **200 OK with an error body** for auth failures — clients rely on the status code.

sections.title: Status Codes for Auth Failures
sections.content:
blue|401 Unauthorized|~Really 'unauthenticated'|no/invalid credentials|re-login fixes it|maps to authentication
rose|403 Forbidden|~Known but blocked|lacks the required role|re-login won't help|maps to authorization
amber|404 Not Found|~Stealth option|hide resource existence|prevents enumeration|used for sensitive resources
emerald|Never|~Avoid|200 OK + error body|breaks clients|always use the status code

sections.title: 401 vs 403 (vs 404)
sections.content:
| | 401 Unauthorized | 403 Forbidden | 404 (sometimes) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Real meaning | Not authenticated | Authenticated but no permission | Hide existence |
| Cause | Missing/invalid/expired credentials | Insufficient role/permission | Avoid leaking a resource |
| Will re-login help? | Yes | No | N/A |
| Maps to | Authentication | Authorization | Authorization (stealth) |
| Spring source | `AuthenticationEntryPoint` | `AccessDeniedHandler` | custom |

sections.title: Returning the Right Status in Spring
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **403 for a missing token**: that's authentication — use **401**.
- **401 for a permission denial**: the user is known, so it's **403**.
- **200 OK with an error message**: breaks clients that branch on status codes.
- **Forgetting `WWW-Authenticate` on 401**: it's part of the spec for how to authenticate.
- **Leaking existence**: for sensitive resources, consider **404** over 403 to prevent enumeration.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **401 Unauthorized = authentication failure** (no/invalid credentials) — despite its name, it means *unauthenticated*.
- **403 Forbidden = authorization failure** (authenticated but lacks permission).
- **Re-authenticating fixes 401, not 403.**
- A 401 should carry a **`WWW-Authenticate`** header.
- Some APIs return **404 instead of 403** to hide resource existence.
- Never signal auth failures with **200 OK**.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
There are two main status codes here, and the catch is that their names don't quite match their meaning. For an authentication failure you return 401 Unauthorized. Even though it's named Unauthorized, it actually means unauthenticated — the request has no valid credentials, maybe the token is missing or expired, or the password was wrong. The server doesn't know who you are, so it can't continue. A correct 401 should also include a WWW-Authenticate header telling the client how to authenticate.

For an authorization failure you return 403 Forbidden. Here the user is authenticated — the server knows exactly who they are — but they don't have permission for that specific resource. A regular user hitting an admin-only endpoint is the classic case. The key difference is that re-logging in won't help with a 403, because the problem isn't your identity, it's that your role doesn't grant access. With a 401, re-authenticating with valid credentials is exactly what fixes it.

So the clean mapping is: 401 is about identity, 403 is about permission. A couple of things that make you stand out: first, never return a 200 OK with an error message in the body for an auth failure, because clients rely on the status code to branch. And second, for sensitive resources, some APIs deliberately return a 404 Not Found instead of a 403, so they don't even reveal that the protected resource exists — that prevents attackers from enumerating what's there. In Spring Security, the 401 path is handled by the AuthenticationEntryPoint and the 403 path by the AccessDeniedHandler, and you can customize both to return JSON error bodies.

beats.content: Think of it this way. 401 says: I don't know who you are. 403 says: I know exactly who you are, and the answer is no. The HTTP spec named 401 'Unauthorized' which is confusing — it really means unauthenticated. Don't let the name throw you.

beats.label: production trap
beats.content: production trap: returning 401 for everything because it's simpler. API clients treat them differently — a client that sees 403 should not retry with a new token, but one that sees 401 should. Getting this wrong breaks your client's auth refresh logic.

question: How does Spring Security handle authentication?
title: How Spring Security Handles Authentication – Java Fresher
direct_answer: Spring Security handles authentication through a **filter** (e.g. `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter`) that builds an **`Authentication`** request and passes it to the **`AuthenticationManager`** (usually `ProviderManager`). The manager delegates to an **`AuthenticationProvider`** (`DaoAuthenticationProvider`), which calls your **`UserDetailsService`** to load the user and a **`PasswordEncoder`** to verify the password. On success it stores a fully-populated `Authentication` in the **`SecurityContextHolder`**; on failure it throws an `AuthenticationException` (→ 401).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can name the collaboration: filter -> AuthenticationManager -> AuthenticationProvider -> UserDetailsService + PasswordEncoder -> SecurityContext
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking authentication happens in the controller, or not knowing UserDetailsService/PasswordEncoder are the extension points
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Trace the object flow end to end and point out that the populated Authentication lands in the SecurityContext for the rest of the request

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Authentication runs in the **filter chain**, before controllers.
- Flow: **filter → AuthenticationManager (ProviderManager) → AuthenticationProvider → UserDetailsService + PasswordEncoder**.
- **`DaoAuthenticationProvider`** loads the user and verifies the password hash.
- Success stores a populated **`Authentication`** in the **`SecurityContextHolder`**; failure → **401**.
- You typically implement only **`UserDetailsService`** and define a **`PasswordEncoder`** bean.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Security handles authentication inside the filter chain, before your controller ever runs, and it's really a chain of collaborators rather than one big method. It starts with an authentication filter — for a username and password login that's the UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter. That filter takes the incoming credentials and wraps them in an Authentication object, but it doesn't verify them itself. It hands that off to the AuthenticationManager, whose default implementation is called ProviderManager.

The manager then delegates to one or more AuthenticationProviders. For username and password, the relevant one is DaoAuthenticationProvider, and this is where the real work happens. It calls your UserDetailsService to load the user from the database by username, and then it uses the PasswordEncoder to check the submitted password against the stored hash. Those two pieces — the UserDetailsService and the PasswordEncoder bean — are usually the only parts you actually implement; Spring orchestrates everything else.

If the password matches, the provider returns a fully authenticated Authentication object that now carries the user's roles, and the filter stores that in the SecurityContextHolder. That's important because the rest of the request, including authorization checks and your service layer, can read who the current user is from there. If verification fails, an AuthenticationException is thrown, and Spring translates that into a 401 Unauthorized response. So the end-to-end story is: filter builds the token, manager delegates to a provider, the provider loads the user and checks the password, and on success the result lands in the security context for the rest of the request.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
**Session-based** auth stores state on the **server**: after login the server keeps a session and the browser holds a **session ID cookie**, which it sends on each request. **Token-based** auth is **stateless**: the server issues a signed **token (JWT)** the client stores and sends in the **`Authorization` header**, and the server validates it without storing anything.

Sessions are simple and easy to revoke but don't scale horizontally without shared session storage; tokens scale well and suit APIs/mobile but are harder to revoke before expiry.

On success it stores a fully-populated `Authentication` in the **`SecurityContextHolder`**; on failure it throws an `AuthenticationException` (→ 401).

sections.title: The Two Beans You Provide
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Authenticating in the controller**: identity verification belongs in the filter chain, not your handler.
- **No `PasswordEncoder` bean**: causes `There is no PasswordEncoder mapped for the id "null"` at runtime.
- **Comparing raw passwords**: never `equals()` passwords — use `PasswordEncoder.matches`.
- **Returning `null` from `loadUserByUsername`**: throw `UsernameNotFoundException` instead.
- **Confusing `AuthenticationManager` and `AuthenticationProvider`**: the manager delegates; the provider does the actual check.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: **Authentication** answers *"who are you?"* — it verifies identity by validating credentials (password, token). **Authorization** answers *"what are you allowed to do?"* — it checks permissions/roles **after** identity is confirmed. They're sequential: authentication always comes first, because you can't grant permissions to an unknown user. The clean mnemonic for interviews: failed authentication returns **401 Unauthorized**, failed authorization returns **403 Forbidden**.

speakable_v2.hook: Spring Security authentication is a relay race: a filter hands off to a manager, which hands off to a provider, which loads your user and checks the password.

beats.label: filter chain steps
beats.content:
Every request enters the filter chain before reaching your controller. The key players in order:
- UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter (or your custom JWT filter) extracts credentials
- AuthenticationManager delegates to DaoAuthenticationProvider
- DaoAuthenticationProvider calls YOUR UserDetailsService to load the user from the database
- BCryptPasswordEncoder verifies the password
- If all passes, the authenticated result goes into SecurityContextHolder
- The request finally reaches your controller with a known identity

beats.label: jwt variant
beats.content: For stateless JWT REST APIs the pattern shifts slightly. Your custom OncePerRequestFilter reads the Bearer token from the Authorization header, validates the signature and expiry, extracts the username from the claims, then loads UserDetails and sets the SecurityContext. No session is created. The SecurityContext lives only for the duration of that request.

beats.label: candidates miss
beats.content: candidates miss: @PreAuthorize does not do authentication. It does authorization. Authentication is done by the filter chain long before your method is invoked.

question: What is role-based access control (RBAC) and how do you implement it in Spring Boot?
title: Role-Based Access Control in Spring Boot – Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)** grants permissions based on **roles** (ADMIN, USER, MANAGER) rather than per-user, so you assign users to roles and protect resources by role. In Spring Boot you implement it by loading each user's roles as **`GrantedAuthority`** objects (with the **`ROLE_`** prefix), then enforcing access with **`hasRole()`** in the `SecurityFilterChain` and/or **`@PreAuthorize`** on methods. The benefit is **central, scalable permission management** — change a role's access once, not per user.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can describe RBAC conceptually and wire it in Spring (authorities + ROLE_ prefix + hasRole/@PreAuthorize)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting the ROLE_ prefix, hardcoding per-user checks, or confusing roles with fine-grained authorities
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish roles (coarse) from authorities/permissions (fine), and show both URL-level and method-level enforcement

sections.title: Permissions by Role, Not by Person
sections.content:
**Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)** assigns permissions to **roles** and assigns **users to roles**, instead of granting permissions to individuals one by one. A user gets access *because of the role they hold*. This makes permissions **central and scalable**: onboard a new manager by giving them the `MANAGER` role; change what managers can do once, and every manager is updated.

In Spring Security, a role is just a **`GrantedAuthority`** string with the conventional **`ROLE_`** prefix (`ROLE_ADMIN`). You load these authorities for the user in your `UserDetailsService`, then enforce access in two places: **URL-level** with `hasRole("ADMIN")` in the `SecurityFilterChain`, and **method-level** with `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")` on service methods.

A useful distinction: **roles** are coarse buckets (ADMIN, USER), while **authorities/permissions** can be fine-grained (`READ_REPORT`, `EDIT_ORDER`). `hasRole('X')` checks for `ROLE_X`; `hasAuthority('READ_REPORT')` checks the exact string with no prefix.

sections.title: RBAC in Spring Boot
sections.content:
blue|Roles|~Coarse buckets|ROLE_ADMIN, ROLE_USER|assigned to users|hasRole('ADMIN')
emerald|Authorities|~Fine-grained|READ_REPORT, EDIT_ORDER|exact string match|hasAuthority('READ_REPORT')
violet|Enforcement|~Two layers|URL: SecurityFilterChain|method: @PreAuthorize|deny by default
amber|Why RBAC|~Scales|change role once|not per user|central management

sections.title: Anti-pattern: per-user and missing prefix
RBAC: roles as authorities + declarative checks
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Dropping the `ROLE_` prefix**: store `ADMIN` but add it as `ROLE_ADMIN`; `hasRole('ADMIN')` checks `ROLE_ADMIN`.
- **`hasRole('ROLE_ADMIN')`**: becomes `ROLE_ROLE_ADMIN` — pass the name without the prefix to `hasRole`.
- **Per-user hardcoded checks**: not RBAC and unmaintainable.
- **Confusing roles and authorities**: `hasRole` adds the prefix; `hasAuthority` matches the exact string.
- **No deny-by-default**: end rules with `anyRequest().authenticated()` so nothing is accidentally public.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **RBAC grants access by role**, assigning users to roles rather than permissions per user.
- Roles are **`GrantedAuthority`** strings with the **`ROLE_`** prefix in Spring Security.
- Enforce at **URL level** (`hasRole`) and **method level** (`@PreAuthorize`).
- **`hasRole('X')`** checks `ROLE_X`; **`hasAuthority('Y')`** matches the exact string.
- RBAC gives **central, scalable** permission management.
- End rules with **deny-by-default** (`anyRequest().authenticated()`).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Role-Based Access Control, or RBAC, is a model where you grant permissions to roles rather than to individual users, and then you assign users to those roles. So a user gets access because of the role they hold — like ADMIN, USER, or MANAGER. The big advantage is that it scales and stays maintainable: if you need to change what managers can do, you change it once on the role, and every manager is updated automatically. You never want to be writing checks like if the username is Alice or Bob, because that falls apart the moment a third person needs access.

In Spring Boot, a role is really just a GrantedAuthority — a string — and the convention is that roles carry a ROLE_ prefix, so the ADMIN role is stored internally as ROLE_ADMIN. You load these authorities for the user in your UserDetailsService when the user logs in. A very common fresher bug here is forgetting the prefix: if you add the authority as just ADMIN instead of ROLE_ADMIN, then hasRole ADMIN silently fails to match.

Then you enforce the rules in two places. At the URL level, in your SecurityFilterChain, you say something like requestMatchers slash admin requires hasRole ADMIN. And at the method level, with method security enabled, you put at PreAuthorize hasRole ADMIN directly on a service method. One nuance worth mentioning is the difference between roles and authorities. Roles are coarse buckets, and hasRole automatically adds the ROLE_ prefix for you. Authorities can be fine-grained permissions like READ_REPORT, and for those you use hasAuthority, which does an exact string match with no prefix. I'd also always finish my rules with anyRequest authenticated so the default is deny, and nothing is accidentally left open.

beats.content: When a user logs in, your UserDetailsService loads their roles from the database and returns them as GrantedAuthority objects inside UserDetails. beats.content: non-obvious: Spring internally stores roles as ROLE_ADMIN, ROLE_USER. hasRole('ADMIN') adds the ROLE_ prefix automatically. hasAuthority('ROLE_ADMIN') does not. Use hasRole() and store without the prefix in your DB to avoid double-prefix bugs.

question: How does session-based authentication differ from token-based authentication?
title: Session vs Token Authentication – Java Backend Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **Session-based** auth stores state on the **server**: after login the server keeps a session and the browser holds a **session ID cookie**, which it sends on each request. **Token-based** auth is **stateless**: the server issues a signed **token (JWT)** the client stores and sends in the **`Authorization` header**, and the server validates it without storing anything. Sessions are simple and easy to revoke but don't scale horizontally without shared session storage; tokens scale well and suit APIs/mobile but are harder to revoke before expiry.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand server-side state vs stateless validation and the scaling/revocation trade-offs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying tokens are 'just better' without the revocation downside; not knowing sessions need sticky/shared storage to scale
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect statelessness to horizontal scaling and to CSRF exposure (cookie vs header), and mention refresh tokens for revocation

sections.title: Server Remembers vs Client Carries Proof
sections.content:
The fundamental difference is **where the authentication state lives**.

In **session-based** authentication, the server is **stateful**: after you log in, it creates a **session** in memory or a store and hands the browser a **session-ID cookie** (`JSESSIONID`). On each request the browser auto-sends that cookie, and the server looks up the session to know who you are. It's simple and **easy to revoke** (delete the session), but the state ties a user to a server — to scale across many servers you need **sticky sessions or shared session storage** (e.g. Redis).

In **token-based** authentication, the server is **stateless**: at login it issues a **signed token (JWT)** containing the user's identity and roles. The client stores it and sends it in the **`Authorization: Bearer`** header. The server just **verifies the signature** — no lookup, no stored state — so any server can handle any request, which scales beautifully and fits **APIs and mobile**. The cost is **revocation**: a valid JWT works until it expires, so you add **short lifetimes plus refresh tokens** or a denylist.

sections.title: Session vs Token at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Session-based|~Stateful server|JSESSIONID cookie|easy to revoke|needs shared store to scale
emerald|Token-based|~Stateless server|JWT in Authorization header|scales horizontally|hard to revoke early
violet|CSRF|~Side effect|cookie auto-sent = exposed|header = immune|drives the design
amber|Pick by use|~Match the app|sessions: web apps|tokens: APIs/mobile|refresh tokens for revocation

sections.title: Session vs Token Authentication
sections.content:
| Aspect | Session-based | Token-based (JWT) |
|---|---|---|
| State | On server (stateful) | None on server (stateless) |
| Client holds | Session-ID cookie | Signed token (JWT) |
| Sent via | Cookie (auto) | `Authorization` header |
| Validation | Lookup session store | Verify signature |
| Scaling | Needs sticky/shared store | Scales horizontally easily |
| Revocation | Easy (delete session) | Hard (wait for expiry/denylist) |
| CSRF | Exposed (cookie auto-sent) | Largely immune (header) |
| Best for | Server-rendered web apps | REST APIs, mobile, SPAs |

sections.title: Session-based: stateful, cookie-driven
sections.content:
```java
// Default Spring Security: server keeps a session, cookie carries JSESSIONID
http
    .formLogin(Customizer.withDefaults())
    .sessionManagement(sm -> sm
        .sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.IF_REQUIRED)); // server stores state
// To scale, you'd add Spring Session + Redis so all nodes share the session.
```

sections.title: Token-based: stateless, header-driven
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Session = server-side state + cookie**; **token = stateless + signed JWT in a header**.
- Sessions are **easy to revoke** but need **sticky/shared storage** to scale across servers.
- Tokens **scale horizontally** and suit APIs/mobile, but are **hard to revoke before expiry**.
- Mitigate token revocation with **short lifetimes + refresh tokens** (or a denylist).
- Cookies are **auto-sent** (CSRF-exposed); header tokens are **largely CSRF-immune**.
- Choose **sessions for server-rendered apps**, **tokens for stateless APIs**.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The fundamental difference between session-based and token-based authentication is where the authentication state lives. In session-based auth, the server is stateful. After you log in, the server creates a session — in memory or in a store — and gives your browser a session ID cookie, usually called JSESSIONID. On every request, the browser automatically sends that cookie, and the server looks up the session to figure out who you are. It's simple, and it's easy to revoke because you just delete the session on the server. The downside is scaling: because the state is tied to a specific server, if you run multiple servers you need either sticky sessions or a shared session store like Redis so any server can find the session.

In token-based auth, the server is stateless. When you log in, the server issues a signed token — typically a JWT — that contains your identity and roles. The client stores that token and sends it on each request in the Authorization header as a Bearer token. The server just verifies the signature; it doesn't store anything or do a lookup. That means any server can handle any request, so it scales horizontally very easily, and it's a great fit for REST APIs, single-page apps, and mobile clients. The trade-off is revocation: a valid JWT keeps working until it expires, so you can't instantly invalidate one. The usual mitigation is short token lifetimes plus refresh tokens, or maintaining a denylist of revoked tokens.

There's also a security angle worth mentioning. Because sessions ride on cookies that the browser sends automatically, they're exposed to CSRF, which is why Spring Security keeps CSRF protection on for them. Token-based APIs that send the token in a header are largely immune to CSRF, because that header isn't auto-attached. So the short version is: sessions for traditional server-rendered web apps, tokens for stateless APIs.

beats.label: tradeoff table
beats.content:
| | Session-based | JWT (token-based) |
|---|---|---|
| Server state | Yes (DB or Redis) | No |
| Revocation | Easy (delete session) | Hard (wait for expiry) |
| Horizontal scaling | Needs shared store | Native |
| Best for | Traditional web apps | REST APIs, microservices |

beats.label: rest apis choose jwt
beats.content: REST APIs should be stateless, so JWT is the natural fit. Any server in the cluster can validate the signature without talking to a database. Configure Spring Security with SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS and CSRF disabled.

beats.label: gotcha
beats.content: gotcha: JWT revocation is non-trivial. A stolen token is valid until it expires. The standard solution is short expiry (15-30 minutes) combined with a long-lived refresh token. A Redis blacklist works but reintroduces state.
